claim: In Escherichia coli, a single pair of replisomes is responsible for duplicating the entire 4.6 Mbp circular chromosome.
source: In Escherichia coli, a single pair of replisomes is responsible for duplicating the entire 4.6 Mbp circular chromosome.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known fact about E. coli chromosome replication.

claim: In vitro studies of reconstituted E. coli replisomes have attributed the remarkable processivity of replisomes to the high stability of the replisome once assembled on DNA.
source: In vitro studies of reconstituted E. coli replisomes have attributed this remarkable processivity to the high stability of the replisome once assembled on DNA.
evidence: This claim references prior in vitro studies and their conclusions about replisome stability.

claim: The Pol III* subassembly frequently disengages from the replisome during DNA synthesis and exchanges with free copies from solution.
source: By examining replisomes in live E. coli with fluorescence microscopy, we found that the Pol III* subassembly frequently disengages from the replisome during DNA synthesis and exchanges with free copies from solution.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on fluorescence microscopy experiments in live cells.

claim: The DnaB helicase associates stably with the replication fork.
source: In contrast, the DnaB helicase associates stably with the replication fork, providing the molecular basis for how the E. coli replisome can maintain high processivity and yet possess the flexibility to bypass obstructions in template DNA.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on fluorescence microscopy experiments.

claim: The E. coli replisome maintains high processivity while possessing flexibility to bypass obstructions in template DNA through stable DnaB association.
source: In contrast, the DnaB helicase associates stably with the replication fork, providing the molecular basis for how the E. coli replisome can maintain high processivity and yet possess the flexibility to bypass obstructions in template DNA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings regarding DnaB stability and its functional implications.

claim: Synthesis of both leading and lagging strands is frequently interrupted in E. coli chromosome replication.
source: Our data challenges the widely-accepted semi-discontinuous model of chromosomal replication, instead supporting a fully discontinuous mechanism in which synthesis of both leading and lagging strands is frequently interrupted.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing frequent Pol III* exchange.

claim: The E. coli replisome is composed of more than 12 different proteins.
source: The E. coli replisome has been characterized in vitro and in vivo and is composed of more than 12 different proteins (Kurth and O'Donnell, 2013; Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Three copies of Pol III are incorporated into the replisome through an interaction with the τ subunit of the pentameric clamp loader complex.
source: Three copies of Pol III are incorporated into the replisome through an interaction with the τ subunit of the pentameric clamp loader complex (τ3δδ').
evidence: This describes the known architecture of the replisome.

claim: The clamp loader is responsible for loading the β clamp dimer onto DNA, which is required for processive synthesis by Pol III.
source: The clamp loader is also responsible for loading the β clamp dimer onto DNA, which is required for processive synthesis by Pol III.
evidence: This describes the known function of the clamp loader in DNA replication.

claim: The DnaB helicase encircles the lagging strand template and unwinds parental DNA.
source: At the core of the E. coli replisome is the replicative helicase, DnaB, which encircles the lagging strand template and unwinds parental DNA.
evidence: This describes the known function and mechanism of DnaB helicase.

claim: The Pol III holoenzyme associates with DnaB through the τ subunit of the clamp loader.
source: The Pol III holoenzyme associates with DnaB through the τ subunit of the clamp loader (Figure 1A).
evidence: This describes the known protein-protein interaction in the replisome, supported by a figure.

claim: Replication of the circular chromosome of E. coli proceeds bidirectionally from a single, defined locus: oriC.
source: Replication of the circular chromosome of E. coli proceeds bidirectionally from a single, defined locus: oriC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about E. coli chromosome replication.

claim: Multiple mechanisms tightly restrict DnaB loading to the oriC locus during initiation, with a single initiation event per cell cycle.
source: Multiple mechanisms tightly restrict DnaB loading, and therefore replisome assembly, to the oriC locus during initiation, with a single initiation event per cell cycle (Costa et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Two sister replisomes are assembled at oriC during initiation, and each is responsible for replicating half of the ~4.6 Mbp chromosome.
source: Two sister replisomes are assembled at oriC during initiation, and each is responsible for replicating half of the ~4.6 Mbp chromosome.
evidence: This describes the known mechanism of bidirectional replication in E. coli.

claim: At 37°C, it takes 40–60 min of continuous DNA synthesis to complete chromosomal replication in E. coli, at rates of 600–1000 bp s−1.
source: At 37°C, it takes 40–60 min of continuous DNA synthesis to complete chromosomal replication, at rates of 600–1000 bp s−1.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about E. coli replication kinetics.

claim: A single purified replisome, once assembled on DNA, is capable of synthesizing DNA with an average length of 70 kbp without requiring replacement of the Pol III* subassembly or DnaB.
source: This is supported by in vitro data showing that a single purified replisome, once assembled on DNA, is capable of synthesizing DNA with an average length of 70 kbp without requiring replacement of the Pol III* subassembly or DnaB (Tanner et al., 2011; Yao et al., 2009).
evidence: This cites in vitro studies demonstrating replisome processivity.

claim: In vivo experiments suggest infrequent replication fork collapse during chromosome replication in E. coli.
source: Even greater stability has been inferred from in vivo experiments that suggest infrequent replication fork collapse during chromosome replication in E. coli (Maisnier-Patin et al., 2001).
evidence: This cites in vivo experiments that infer replisome stability.

claim: DNA lesions can result in the stalling of the replisome due to Pol III's inability to use damaged DNA as a template.
source: DNA lesions can result in the stalling of the replisome due to Pol III's inability to use damaged DNA as a template (Moore et al., 1981).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: The replisome frequently encounters DNA-bound proteins, potentially resulting in disassembly or pausing.
source: In addition, the replisome frequently encounters DNA-bound proteins, potentially resulting in disassembly or pausing (Mettrick and Grainge, 2016; Gupta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: The bound-time for the α subunit of Pol III was 4 ± 2 seconds.
source: The bound-time was 4 ± 2 and 6 ± 2 s (mean ± SE) for the α and ε subunits of Pol III, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from FRAP experiments.

claim: The bound-time for the ε subunit of Pol III was 6 ± 2 seconds.
source: The bound-time was 4 ± 2 and 6 ± 2 s (mean ± SE) for the α and ε subunits of Pol III, respectively.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from FRAP experiments.

claim: The τ, δ and χ subunits of the clamp loader had bound times of 6 ± 3, 3 ± 2 and 6 ± 4 s, respectively.
source: Similarly, the τ, δ and χ subunits of the clamp loader had bound times of 6 ± 3, 3 ± 2 and 6 ± 4 s, respectively (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from FRAP experiments, with reference to figures.

claim: Molecules of the β clamp remained associated for an average of 36 ± 21 s.
source: Molecules of the β clamp exchanged at a slower rate, remaining associated for an average of 36 ± 21 s, consistent with its binding to newly-synthesized DNA behind the replisome (Moolman et al., 2014; Su'etsugu and Errington, 2011).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from FRAP experiments, with citations to support the interpretation.

claim: The timescale of Pol III holoenzyme exchange is in striking contrast to the ~150 min required for two replisomes to complete chromosomal replication under the microscopy conditions used.
source: The timescale of Pol III holoenzyme exchange is in striking contrast to the ~150 min required for two replisomes to complete chromosomal replication under our microscopy conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This compares the measured exchange rates to the total replication time measured in the study.

claim: Pol III ε subunit remained bound to the replisome for 10 ± 0.7 seconds as measured by sptPALM.
source: Pol III subunit and clamp loader components indeed exchanged rapidly, with ε, τ and δ remaining replisome-associated for only 10 ± 0.7, 10 ± 0.7 and 12 ± 0.9 s (mean ± SE), respectively (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sptPALM experiments.

claim: The τ subunit remained bound to the replisome for 10 ± 0.7 seconds as measured by sptPALM.
source: Pol III subunit and clamp loader components indeed exchanged rapidly, with ε, τ and δ remaining replisome-associated for only 10 ± 0.7, 10 ± 0.7 and 12 ± 0.9 s (mean ± SE), respectively (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sptPALM experiments.

claim: The δ subunit remained bound to the replisome for 12 ± 0.9 seconds as measured by sptPALM.
source: Pol III subunit and clamp loader components indeed exchanged rapidly, with ε, τ and δ remaining replisome-associated for only 10 ± 0.7, 10 ± 0.7 and 12 ± 0.9 s (mean ± SE), respectively (Figure 2B and D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sptPALM experiments.

claim: There is no strong evidence for multiple binding behaviors of individual replisome subunits.
source: We found no strong evidence for multiple binding behaviors of individual subunits (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and Supplementary file 1C), suggesting that both leading and lagging strand polymerases behave similarly.
evidence: This is a conclusion from statistical analysis of the sptPALM data.

claim: Both leading and lagging strand polymerases behave similarly in terms of binding kinetics.
source: We found no strong evidence for multiple binding behaviors of individual subunits (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D and Supplementary file 1C), suggesting that both leading and lagging strand polymerases behave similarly.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of multiple binding behaviors in the data.

claim: The unit of exchange of Pol III and clamp loader subunits is the Pol III* subassembly ((αεθ)3-τ3δδ').
source: We therefore propose that the unit of exchange of Pol III and clamp loader subunits is the Pol III* subassembly ((αεθ)3-τ3δδ').
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the similar exchange rates of all subunits despite different stoichiometries.

claim: In vitro data shows that exchange of Pol III at the replication fork requires it to be part of the Pol III* subassembly.
source: This idea is supported by in vitro data that shows that exchange of Pol III at the replication fork requires it to be part of the Pol III* subassembly (Yuan et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites in vitro data supporting the proposed model.

claim: Cells have an excess of free Pol III that does not interact with the clamp loader.
source: Cells have an excess of free Pol III that does not interact with the clamp loader (Maki and Kornberg, 1985).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Re-binding of single molecules of ε occurs at a much higher frequency than would be predicted if all of the ~270 molecules of ε in the cell were in direct competition.
source: Consistent with the notion that only Pol III subunits found within a Pol III* subassembly are competent for exchange, we observed re-binding of single molecules of ε, often to a different replisome, at a much higher frequency than would be predicted if all of the ~270 molecules of ε in the cell were in direct competition (Reyes-Lamothe et al., 2010) (Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an observation from sptPALM experiments that supports the model of Pol III* exchange.

claim: The β clamp showed a bound-time of 47 ± 3 s in sptPALM.
source: The β clamp again showed a longer bound-time of 47 ± 3 s in sptPALM.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sptPALM experiments.

claim: A new β dimer is loaded at each replication fork every ~2 s.
source: Assuming similar numbers of DNA-bound β as in that earlier report, we estimate from our results that a new β dimer is loaded at each replication fork every ~2 s.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured β clamp bound-time and assumptions about the number of bound β clamps.

claim: The average Okazaki fragment length is 520 bp under the experimental conditions used.
source: Considering an average rate of fork progression of ~260 bp s−1 – calculated from the duration of replication in the conditions used (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) – we find an average Okazaki fragment length of 520 bp, in close agreement with an in vitro measurement of 650 bp at room temperature (Yao et al., 2009).
evidence: This is calculated from the measured fork progression rate and β clamp loading rate, and compared to in vitro measurements.

claim: The average replication fork progression is 1–3 kbp prior to Pol III exchange.
source: In contrast, we estimate from FRAP and sptPALM an average replication fork progression of 1–3 kbp prior to Pol III exchange, which would allow completion of multiple Okazaki cycles.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured Pol III exchange rates and fork progression rate.

claim: Subunit exchange within the replisome is unlikely to be exclusively linked to the dynamics on the lagging strand.
source: We therefore think it unlikely that subunit exchange within the replisome is exclusively linked to the dynamics on the lagging strand.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Pol III exchange occurs less frequently than Okazaki fragment synthesis.

claim: Full fluorescence recovery of DnaB was never observed over 5 min of measurement in FRAP experiments.
source: Crucially, we never observed full fluorescence recovery of DnaB over 5 min of measurement (Figure 1B–D), indicating that it is stably associated with the replisome on this timescale.
evidence: This is a direct observation from FRAP experiments.

claim: DnaB is stably associated with the replisome on a timescale of at least 5 minutes.
source: Crucially, we never observed full fluorescence recovery of DnaB over 5 min of measurement (Figure 1B–D), indicating that it is stably associated with the replisome on this timescale.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of fluorescence recovery in FRAP experiments.

claim: In contrast to Pol III holoenzyme subunits, replisome-associated DnaB does not exchange frequently.
source: We conclude that in contrast to Pol III holoenzyme subunits, replisome-associated DnaB does not exchange frequently, and is instead a stable component of the replisome.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing DnaB FRAP results to those of other replisome subunits.

claim: DnaB is a stable component of the replisome.
source: We conclude that in contrast to Pol III holoenzyme subunits, replisome-associated DnaB does not exchange frequently, and is instead a stable component of the replisome.
evidence: This is a conclusion from FRAP experiments showing lack of DnaB exchange.

claim: Single molecules of DnaB remained bound to the replisome for 913 ± 508 s as measured by sptPALM.
source: Crucially, we estimate that single molecules of DnaB remained bound to the replisome for 913 ± 508 s, significantly longer than any other component (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from sptPALM experiments.

claim: DnaB is the most stable subunit in the replisome.
source: Analysis of DnaB by sptPALM confirmed that it is the most stable subunit in the replisome.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing DnaB sptPALM results to those of other replisome subunits.

claim: DnaB is the primary determinant of replisome integrity.
source: Altogether, our data supports a role for DnaB as the primary determinant of replisome integrity.
evidence: This is a conclusion inferred from the stability of DnaB compared to other replisome components.

claim: Components of the Pol III* subassembly showed bound-times two- to six fold higher in cells treated with hydroxyurea compared to untreated cells.
source: Components of the Pol III* subassembly and the β-clamp showed bound-times two- to six fold higher than in untreated cells (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from FRAP and sptPALM experiments with hydroxyurea treatment.

claim: The β-clamp showed bound-times two- to six fold higher in cells treated with hydroxyurea compared to untreated cells.
source: Components of the Pol III* subassembly and the β-clamp showed bound-times two- to six fold higher than in untreated cells (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from FRAP and sptPALM experiments with hydroxyurea treatment.

claim: Hydroxyurea had no apparent effect on DnaB FRAP estimates.
source: HU had no apparent effect on DnaB FRAP estimates (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from FRAP experiments with hydroxyurea treatment.

claim: The exchange of replisome components is at least partially dependent on active DNA synthesis.
source: We conclude that the exchange of replisome components is at least partially dependent on active DNA synthesis.
evidence: This is concluded from the observation that hydroxyurea treatment increases bound-times.

claim: The replisome may be intrinsically dynamic as a multiprotein complex, with DNA synthesis further increasing subunit exchange.
source: In addition, it may indicate that the replisome is intrinsically dynamic as a multiprotein complex, with DNA synthesis further increasing subunit exchange.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of exchange based on the observation that exchange still occurs (albeit at reduced rates) when synthesis is inhibited.

claim: Bypass of obstacles on DNA could be achieved through detachment of the stalled Pol III* subassembly from DnaB and its replacement downstream of the obstacle with another Pol III* from solution.
source: Our data is entirely consistent with this mechanism, whereby bypass could be achieved through detachment of the stalled Pol III* subassembly from DnaB and its replacement downstream of the obstacle with another Pol III* from solution.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings and in vitro studies.

claim: Small lesions and large protein blockages on the leading strand can both be bypassed by Pol III* exchange because DnaB translocates on the lagging strand.
source: Because DnaB translocates on the lagging strand, small lesions and large protein blockages on the leading strand can both be bypassed by Pol III* exchange.
evidence: This is inferred from the known mechanism of DnaB translocation and the observed Pol III* exchange.

claim: Inhibiting transcription had no apparent effect on the dynamics of Pol III.
source: Note however that we did not observe any apparent effect on the dynamics of Pol III after inhibiting transcription, suggesting that this process is not the main cause of exchange (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a result from experiments with rifampicin treatment.

claim: Transcription is not the main cause of Pol III exchange.
source: Note however that we did not observe any apparent effect on the dynamics of Pol III after inhibiting transcription, suggesting that this process is not the main cause of exchange (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of effect of rifampicin on Pol III dynamics.

claim: Obstacle bypass along template DNA may be the primary selection pressure that has driven the evolution of a dynamic replisome.
source: We propose that obstacle bypass along template DNA may be the primary selection pressure that has driven the evolution of a dynamic replisome.
evidence: This is a proposed evolutionary explanation for the observed dynamics.

claim: Unbinding of Pol III* subassembly may result from build-up of helical torsion in the template DNA generated by the coupled synthesis of both DNA strands.
source: First, unbinding of Pol III* subassembly may result from build-up of helical torsion in the template DNA generated by the coupled synthesis of both DNA strands (Kurth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a proposed alternative mechanism for Pol III* exchange, with a supporting citation.

claim: Longer binding times when synthesis was inhibited by HU is consistent with unbinding resulting from helical torsion build-up.
source: This is consistent with longer binding times when synthesis was inhibited by HU.
evidence: This connects the hydroxyurea results to the proposed torsion mechanism.

claim: The observed dynamics may be a byproduct of the highly regulated interaction between Pol III and β-clamp.
source: Second, the dynamics observed may be a byproduct of the highly regulated interaction between Pol III and β-clamp.
evidence: This is a proposed alternative mechanism for the observed dynamics.

claim: Pol III tightly binds the β-clamp to ensure highly processive synthesis.
source: Even though Pol III tightly binds the β-clamp to ensure highly processive synthesis, these two proteins rapidly unbind from each other upon completion of the duplex DNA.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Pol III-β clamp interaction.

claim: Pol III and β-clamp rapidly unbind from each other upon completion of the duplex DNA.
source: Even though Pol III tightly binds the β-clamp to ensure highly processive synthesis, these two proteins rapidly unbind from each other upon completion of the duplex DNA.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the Pol III-β clamp interaction.

claim: The strength of the Pol III-β clamp interaction is modulated by the OB domain in the α subunit of Pol III and the C-terminus of the τ subunit of the clamp loader.
source: The strength of this protein-protein interaction is modulated by the OB domain in the α subunit of Pol III, which binds to ssDNA ahead of the catalytic domain, and the C-terminus of the τ subunit of the clamp loader (Georgescu et al., 2009, Leu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: Premature activation of the Pol III-β clamp dissociation switch in both leading and lagging strand polymerases would weaken the grip of the Pol III* subassembly on the replication fork and potentially result in its displacement.
source: Premature activation of such a switch in both leading and lagging strand polymerases would weaken the grip of the Pol III* subassembly on the replication fork and potentially result in its displacement.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism for Pol III* exchange.

claim: The presence of ssDNA gaps in the lagging strand is consistent with premature loss of Pol III processivity.
source: This idea is consistent with the presence of ssDNA gaps in the lagging strand (Li and Marians, 2000), which may be explained by a premature loss of Pol III processivity.
evidence: This connects published observations to the proposed mechanism, with a supporting citation.

claim: Exchange of Pol III* subassembly within the replisome presumably occurs rapidly enough to minimize potentially deleterious ssDNA gaps between fragments of nascent DNA on the leading strand.
source: Presumably, exchange of Pol III* subassembly within the replisome occurs rapidly enough to minimize potentially deleterious ssDNA gaps between fragments of nascent DNA on the leading strand.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional consequences of the observed exchange rates.

claim: The rate of DNA unwinding by DnaB decreases by more than 10-fold when DnaB is detached from the τ subunit of the clamp loader.
source: However, the rate of DNA unwinding by DnaB decreases by more than 10-fold when DnaB is detached from the τ subunit of the clamp loader (Kim et al., 1996a), providing a potential safety mechanism to limit DNA unwinding and exposure of ssDNA during Pol III* subassembly exchange.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation, and its functional implication is inferred.

claim: The decreased rate of DNA unwinding by DnaB when detached from τ provides a potential safety mechanism to limit DNA unwinding and exposure of ssDNA during Pol III* subassembly exchange.
source: However, the rate of DNA unwinding by DnaB decreases by more than 10-fold when DnaB is detached from the τ subunit of the clamp loader (Kim et al., 1996a), providing a potential safety mechanism to limit DNA unwinding and exposure of ssDNA during Pol III* subassembly exchange.
evidence: This is a proposed functional implication of the known DnaB behavior.

claim: In vitro measurements were performed by removing all diffusing Pol III* subassembly and DnaB subunits from the reaction.
source: Measurements in those reports were performed by removing all diffusing Pol III* subassembly and DnaB subunits from the reaction.
evidence: This describes the conditions of the in vitro studies being compared to the in vivo results.

claim: In the cell there is a permanent excess of diffusing replisome subunits.
source: In contrast, in the cell there is a permanent excess of diffusing replisome subunits.
evidence: This is stated as a known difference between in vitro and in vivo conditions.

claim: The presence of excess diffusing subunits in cells explains the differences observed between in vitro and in vivo data.
source: We believe this explains the differences observed with our in vivo data.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for the discrepancy between in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: Competition for binding sites between DNA-bound and diffusing molecules has been shown to change the DNA-binding kinetics of proteins such as Fis, HU and NHP6A.
source: Competition for binding sites between DNA-bound and diffusing molecules has been shown to change the DNA-binding kinetics of proteins such as Fis, HU and NHP6A (Graham et al., 2011), EcoRI (Sidorova et al., 2013), RPA (Gibb et al., 2014) and the transcription factor CueR (Chen et al., 2015).
evidence: This cites multiple studies showing that competition affects binding kinetics of various proteins.

claim: Mathematical modelling has shown that it is theoretically possible for a replisome to be stable under conditions in which no extra subunits are present and yet undergo frequent subunit exchange in the presence of extra subunits.
source: Furthermore, mathematical modelling has shown that it is theoretically possible for a replisome to be stable under conditions in which no extra subunits are present, as in vitro, and yet undergo frequent subunit exchange in the presence of extra subunits, as in vivo, due to subunit competition (Åberg et al., 2016).
evidence: This cites a mathematical modeling study supporting the proposed explanation.

claim: Active synthesis may enhance exchange with the diffusing pool.
source: We think that active synthesis may enhance exchange with the diffusing pool, consistent with our results using HU.
evidence: This is inferred from the hydroxyurea results showing increased bound-times when synthesis is inhibited.

claim: Frequent exchange of DNA polymerases in the presence of extra subunits has been observed in the replisomes of bacteriophages T4 and T7 in vitro.
source: Frequent exchange of DNA polymerases in the presence of extra subunits has been observed in the replisomes of bacteriophages T4 and T7 in vitro (Yang et al., 2004; Johnson et al., 2007).
evidence: This cites in vitro studies of bacteriophage replisomes showing similar exchange behavior.

claim: In T7, polymerase exchange occurs through a mechanism in which extra DNA polymerases associate with the bacteriophage DNA helicase and exchange with the active DNA polymerase through competition for DNA binding.
source: In T7, this occurs through a mechanism in which extra DNA polymerases associate with the bacteriophage DNA helicase and exchange with the active DNA polymerase through competition for DNA binding (Geertsema et al., 2014; Loparo et al., 2011).
evidence: This cites studies describing the mechanism of polymerase exchange in T7.

claim: One predicted consequence of the Pol III* subassembly exchanging as a single unit is that synthesis of both leading and lagging strands will be frequently interrupted, resulting in discontinuities on both strands.
source: One predicted consequence of the Pol III* subassembly exchanging as a single unit is that synthesis of both leading and lagging strands will be frequently interrupted, resulting in discontinuities on both strands.
evidence: This is a logical consequence inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The semi-discontinuous model of DNA replication is strongly supported by in vitro experiments.
source: However, while this model is strongly supported by in vitro experiments (Wu et al., 1992), the mechanism that operates in vivo has long been unclear (Yeeles, 2014; Wang, 2005).
evidence: This cites in vitro studies supporting the semi-discontinuous model and reviews noting uncertainty about the in vivo mechanism.

claim: The mechanism of DNA replication that operates in vivo has long been unclear.
source: However, while this model is strongly supported by in vitro experiments (Wu et al., 1992), the mechanism that operates in vivo has long been unclear (Yeeles, 2014; Wang, 2005).
evidence: This cites reviews noting uncertainty about the in vivo mechanism of DNA replication.

claim: Okazaki and colleagues' original characterization of replication intermediates demonstrated that all DNA is initially synthesized as short fragments, supporting fully discontinuous DNA replication.
source: Okazaki and colleagues' original characterization of replication intermediates demonstrated that all DNA is initially synthesized as short fragments, supporting fully discontinuous DNA replication (Okazaki et al., 1968).
evidence: This cites the original Okazaki experiments and their interpretation.

claim: Recent in vivo experiments performed in the absence of DNA ligase support the idea that discontinuities are produced on both leading and lagging strands during DNA replication in E. coli.
source: More recent in vivo experiments performed in the absence of DNA ligase support the idea that discontinuities are produced on both leading and lagging strands during DNA replication in E. coli (Amado and Kuzminov, 2013, 2006).
evidence: This cites recent in vivo studies supporting discontinuous synthesis on both strands.

claim: The data provide a mechanistic explanation for observations that discontinuities are produced on both leading and lagging strands.
source: Our data provide a mechanistic explanation for these observations, and supports a discontinuous model of DNA synthesis in E. coli.
evidence: This connects the experimental findings to previous observations, providing a mechanistic explanation.

claim: The data support a discontinuous model of DNA synthesis in E. coli.
source: Our data provide a mechanistic explanation for these observations, and supports a discontinuous model of DNA synthesis in E. coli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Treatment with cephalexin did not affect DNA replication.
source: To minimize photobleaching of the diffusing pool of fluorescent proteins we increased cell volume by treatment with cephalexin; this did not affect DNA replication (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a control result with reference to a figure showing the data.

claim: Fluorescence recovery in FRAP experiments represents protein exchange, not photophysical properties of YPet like photoblinking.
source: Fluorescence recovery is not explained by the photophysical properties of YPet, like photoblinking, and instead it represents protein exchange (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a control result with reference to a figure showing the data.

claim: The replication time under microscopy conditions was approximately 150 minutes.
source: The timescale of Pol III holoenzyme exchange is in striking contrast to the ~150 min required for two replisomes to complete chromosomal replication under our microscopy conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a measured value from the experiments, with reference to a figure.

claim: Gene fusions to fluorescent proteins did not have any apparent detrimental effect on cell growth.
source: Gene fusions did not have any apparent detrimental effect on cell growth (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a control result with reference to a figure showing growth curves.

claim: The illumination protocol used for sptPALM did not perturb cell growth.
source: This illumination protocol did not perturb cell growth (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated as a control result with reference to a figure showing cell growth during imaging.
